Fixed Tangent Point

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: Move a dot along a line and watch a circle that always goes through one fixed dot.
How to play: Drag O, R, X or P, or focus a dot with Tab and use the arrow keys. Press Names, Hint or Statement to show more of the picture.
Look for the math

Drag the dot P along the line. Its circle shrinks and grows, yet the red dot Q never moves. This is a droodle: a picture that hides a theorem. R. Honsberger credited Hiroshi Haruki with the result. There is nothing to win — the point is to see why the red dot stays put.

The claim on the page

Given a circle C with centre O and a line m that does not meet it, there is a point Q such that PQ = PT for every point P on m, where PT is the length of the tangent from P to C. So the circle centred at P with radius PT always passes through Q. The logic test checks this at thousands of line heights and positions of P: the largest relative difference it found between PQ and PT is below 1e-10. The live cut-the-knot page now shows only a Java warning; a 2012 Wayback snapshot embeds the FixedTangentPoint applet the text describes.

Four right triangles

Let M be the foot of the perpendicular from O to m, let MN and PT touch the circle, and write r = ON = OT and z = MN. Four right triangles give the whole proof. From OPT and OMP, r² + PT² = OM² + MP². From QMP and OMN, with Q on MO chosen so that MQ = z, OM² + MP² = r² + PQ². Compare the two lines and the r² and OM² terms cancel: PT² = PQ². Both lengths are positive, so PT = PQ. The Pythagorean theorem is the only tool needed; pressing Hint draws those four right angles.

The other fixed point

Once z² = OM² − r² is fixed, so is Q, even though P slides. Reflect Q across the line m and you get a second point Q' with PQ' = PQ. In the language of orthogonal circles, every circle centred on m and orthogonal to C passes through both points; m is their radical axis. The test checks the orthogonality condition OP² = r² + PT² for every case too.

When the picture goes quiet

The page assumes m misses C. If m cuts C, then OM² − r² is negative and the applet's square root is NaN: it keeps the last drawn Q and N instead of showing new ones. If P itself goes inside C, the applet's guard stops the whole redraw. This port keeps both behaviours; the status line says which one happened. The tangent points here come from an analytic formula while the check script compares them with a second transcription of the applet's inversion-and-intersection code, point by point, on random and grid layouts.

Try pressing Hint, then slide P from far left to far right. Next move X towards the circle until the line touches it: watch what happens to Q.
